title: The Spacing Calculator
author: Lee Wheeler
summary: Lee Wheeler argues that most school "retrieval practice" is retrieval in name only -- five-minute starters and spiral-curriculum reviews spaced so far apart that students essentially relearn material from scratch, with topic selection driven by instinct rather than a system. After finding manual spreadsheet scheduling of spaced retrieval intervals unsustainable against real school constraints (holidays, fire alarms, absence), he built the free Spacing Calculator: teachers input "atoms" (individual facts, skills, or concepts, credited to Kris Bolton's atomisation approach), assign a difficulty multiplier between 2 and 3, add lesson dates, and the tool outputs an automatically generated retrieval calendar that snaps to actual lesson dates and adjusts intervals whenever a topic is retaught or a retrieval attempt fails. Wheeler argues the tool requires no extra curriculum time, just the same time spent differently -- spaced rather than blocked -- and reframes systematic retrieval as a design principle rather than an afterthought bolted onto lesson planning.
points: Wheeler's diagnostic claim is stark: at best, students get 2-3 opportunities to retrieve most topics across a whole year at essentially random intervals, when durable memory needs roughly 5 or more properly spaced opportunities.

His manual-spreadsheet failure story is the piece's credibility anchor -- a geometric-progression retrieval schedule (day 2, 4, 8, 16...) collapsed against real-world scheduling chaos (holidays, fire alarms, absence), motivating the automated tool.

The tool's core mechanic -- a difficulty multiplier between 2 and 3 controlling how quickly retrieval intervals expand, capped at 60 days -- mirrors spaced-repetition algorithms like AnkiDroid's, adapted for a fixed school timetable rather than open-ended flashcard review.

Wheeler's response to the "where's the time" objection reframes rather than dismisses it: no extra time is needed, just the same total teaching time distributed as short spaced retrieval chunks instead of blocked single-lesson coverage.
quotes: We see five-minute starters or Do Nows. Five minutes of recall; five minutes of learning. Then the lesson moves on, and the next topic begins.

As a very rough estimate, to help build permanent and resilient memory, we should be aiming for 5 or more opportunities for retrieval of any given topic, spaced close enough that pupils do not forget but the memory still builds.
It was perfect in theory but completely unsustainable in practice, the document was completely overwhelming to look at and basically impossible to understand efficiently.
Between 2 and 3 (can be a decimal), based on difficulty. Harder topics get tighter spacing (a multiplier closer to 2), easier ones get longer intervals (a multiplier closer to 3).
There is enough time in the curriculum to retrieve properly. It just requires reconsidering some entrenched assumptions.
We’ve pretended for too long that retrieval can be done on instinct. It can’t. It needs structure.
